item.title: Solute Uptake by Algal Cells With and Without an Energy Blocker
item.stimulus:
Students studied how cells of a freshwater alga take up a dissolved solute, X. Two groups of algal cells were placed in identical solutions containing X at a concentration of 2.0 mM. The volume of solution was very large, so the external concentration of X stayed at 2.0 mM throughout the experiment. One group (control) received no treatment. The other group was first treated with a compound that blocks the cells' production of ATP and was otherwise handled identically. The students measured the concentration of X inside the cells at several times.

Time (min) | Internal [X], control (mM) | Internal [X], ATP-blocked (mM)
0 | 0.5 | 0.5
10 | 6.5 | 1.4
20 | 12.5 | 1.9
30 | 18.5 | 2.0
40 | 24.5 | 2.0
item.model_answer:
(a) Rate = (18.5 mM − 6.5 mM) ÷ (30 min − 10 min) = 12 mM ÷ 20 min = 0.6 mM/min.

(b) The control cells use active transport. After 10 minutes the internal concentration of X (6.5 mM, rising to 24.5 mM) is higher than the external concentration of 2.0 mM, yet X keeps entering, so it is moving from a region of low concentration to a region of high concentration, against its gradient. The ATP-blocked cells show this requires energy: when ATP production is blocked, the internal concentration levels off at 2.0 mM and never exceeds the outside concentration. Therefore the accumulation in the control cells depends on a direct input of metabolic energy.

(c) Without ATP, X can only move by passive transport. At the start the concentration outside (2.0 mM) is higher than inside (0.5 mM), so there is net movement of X into the cells down its concentration gradient without energy input. Once the internal concentration reaches 2.0 mM, the concentrations are equal, there is no gradient, and there is no further net movement, so the value stays constant.

(d) Blocking ATP production would decrease or stop the uptake of the protein particles. Taking in large particles by folding the membrane inward to form vesicles is endocytosis, which requires energy. Without ATP the cell cannot supply that energy, so fewer particles would be engulfed.

item.title: Solute Accumulation and Energy Use in Algal Cells
item.stimulus:
Researchers studied how cells of a freshwater alga take up solute X, a small, uncharged molecule that the cells do not metabolize. Algal cells with an internal solute X concentration of 1.0 mM were placed in a large volume of medium containing 5.0 mM solute X. Because the medium volume was large, the external concentration stayed at 5.0 mM throughout the experiment. One group of cells (control) received no treatment. A second group was treated with a chemical that blocks the production of ATP in the cells. The internal concentration of solute X was measured every 10 minutes.

Time (min) | Internal solute X, control (mM) | Internal solute X, ATP inhibitor (mM)
0 | 1.0 | 1.0
10 | 6.0 | 3.0
20 | 12.0 | 4.5
30 | 18.0 | 5.0
item.model_answer:
(a) Active transport. Between 10 and 30 minutes the internal concentration in the control rises from 6.0 mM to 18.0 mM while the external concentration is only 5.0 mM. Solute X is therefore moving from a region of lower concentration (outside) to a region of higher concentration (inside), against its concentration gradient, which requires active transport.

(b) Rate = (18.0 mM − 6.0 mM) ÷ (30 min − 10 min) = 12.0 mM ÷ 20 min = 0.60 mM/min.

(c) At first the inside (1.0 mM) is lower than the outside (5.0 mM), so solute X moves into the cells by passive transport, a net movement from high to low concentration that needs no direct input of metabolic energy. When the internal concentration reaches 5.0 mM, the concentrations are equal, there is no gradient, and net movement stops. The concentration cannot go above 5.0 mM because moving solute X from low to high concentration requires active transport, which needs a direct input of energy such as ATP. The inhibitor blocks ATP production, so active transport cannot occur.

(d) Uptake of the protein particles will decrease or stop. Endocytosis requires energy to fold the plasma membrane inward and pinch off vesicles that engulf the particles, and without ATP the cells cannot supply this energy.

item.title: Solute Accumulation and Bead Uptake in Cultured Cells
item.stimulus:
Researchers studied how cultured animal cells take in two kinds of material: solute X, a small polar molecule, and fluorescent beads that are far too large to pass through any membrane protein. At the start, the cells contained no solute X. Cells were divided into two groups and placed in a large volume of medium containing 2.0 mM solute X and fluorescent beads. The medium volume was large enough that the external concentration of X stayed at 2.0 mM throughout. The control group received no treatment. The second group received a compound that stops the cells from producing ATP but does not damage the plasma membrane. After 60 minutes, the researchers measured the concentration of X inside the cells and the percentage of cells containing beads inside vesicles. Earlier time points showed that internal X had stopped changing by 60 minutes in both groups.

Condition | Internal [X] at 60 min (mM) | External [X] (mM) | Cells containing beads (%)
Control | 12.0 | 2.0 | 64
ATP-production blocked | 2.0 | 2.0 | 4
item.model_answer:
(a) Ratio = internal [X] ÷ external [X] = 12.0 mM ÷ 2.0 mM = 6. The control cells hold X at 6 times the outside concentration.

(b) X enters by active transport. In the control cells, X reached 12.0 mM inside while the medium was only 2.0 mM. X was moved from a region of low concentration to a region of high concentration, against its gradient. When ATP production was blocked, internal X rose only to 2.0 mM, equal to the outside. This shows that X can enter passively only until the concentrations are equal, and that accumulation above the external level requires a direct input of energy.

(c) The beads are taken in by endocytosis. The plasma membrane folds inward around the beads and pinches off as vesicles, and this process requires energy. When ATP production was blocked, the cells could not form these vesicles, so the percentage of cells containing beads dropped from 64% to 4%.

(d) Internal X will decrease from 12.0 mM to about 2.0 mM, the same as the medium. Without ATP, active transport stops and can no longer maintain the gradient. The blocked-ATP group shows that X can cross the membrane without energy, so X will show net passive movement out of the cell, from high concentration to low concentration. This continues until the inside and outside concentrations are equal.

item.title: Solute Uptake in Cells With and Without ATP
item.stimulus:
Students studied how cultured animal cells take up solute X, a small polar molecule that crosses the plasma membrane only through membrane proteins. Cells were placed in a large volume of medium in which the concentration of X was held constant at 1.0 mM. Group 1 (control) received no treatment. Group 2 was treated with a compound that blocks ATP production but does not damage the plasma membrane or its proteins. The concentration of X inside the cells was measured over time.

Time (min) | Internal X, Group 1 control (mM) | Internal X, Group 2 ATP blocked (mM)
0 | 0.0 | 0.0
10 | 1.5 | 0.6
20 | 2.8 | 0.9
40 | 4.3 | 1.0
60 | 5.0 | 1.0

The same cells can also engulf fluorescent beads 1 µm in diameter from the medium. The beads are far too large to pass through any membrane protein.
item.model_answer:
(a) Active transport. Between 40 and 60 minutes the internal concentration of X in Group 1 rises from 4.3 mM to 5.0 mM while the external concentration is only 1.0 mM. X is therefore moving from a region of low concentration (outside) to a region of high concentration (inside), against its concentration gradient, which requires active transport.

(b) Ratio = internal ÷ external = 5.0 mM ÷ 1.0 mM = 5.0. Inside the cells, X is 5 times as concentrated as in the medium.

(c) Blocking ATP production removes the energy needed for active transport, so X can enter only by passive transport through membrane proteins. Passive transport produces net movement from high to low concentration, so X moves into the cells only until the internal concentration equals the external concentration of 1.0 mM. At that point there is no net movement, so the level stays at 1.0 mM. Rising above 1.0 mM, as in Group 1, would require moving X against its gradient, which needs energy.

(d) Group 2 cells will take up fewer beads than Group 1 cells, with little or no bead uptake. The beads are too large to pass through membrane proteins, so they must enter by endocytosis, in which the plasma membrane folds inward and forms small vesicles that engulf the beads. Endocytosis requires energy, and with ATP production blocked the cells lack that energy, so bead uptake decreases.

item.title: Solute Accumulation and Energy Use in Cultured Cells
item.stimulus:
Researchers studied how cultured pancreatic cells take up amino acid Q. Q is a polar molecule that cannot cross the phospholipid bilayer directly but enters cells through membrane transport proteins. Two groups of cells were placed in a medium in which the concentration of Q was held constant at 2.0 mM. The control group received no treatment. The treated group received a compound that blocks ATP production. The concentration of Q inside the cells was measured every 10 minutes.

Time (min) | Internal [Q], control cells (mM) | Internal [Q], treated cells (mM)
0 | 0.5 | 0.5
10 | 8.0 | 1.4
20 | 15.5 | 1.9
30 | 22.0 | 2.0

External [Q] for both groups: 2.0 mM at all times.
item.model_answer:
(a) Ratio = internal [Q] ÷ external [Q] = 22.0 mM ÷ 2.0 mM = 11. The control cells hold 11 times more Q inside than outside.

(b) Active transport. After internal [Q] passes 2.0 mM, Q keeps entering the control cells until it reaches 22.0 mM, even though the outside concentration is only 2.0 mM. Q is therefore moving from a region of low concentration to a region of high concentration, against its gradient, which requires the direct input of energy.

(c) The compound blocks ATP production, so the cells cannot perform active transport. Q can still enter by passive transport through transport proteins, which causes net movement from high concentration (2.0 mM outside) to low concentration (0.5 mM inside). As internal [Q] rises, the gradient shrinks, and once the inside reaches 2.0 mM the concentrations are equal, so there is no further net movement and internal [Q] does not exceed 2.0 mM.

(d) Treated cells will secrete less enzyme (secretion will decrease or stop). Exocytosis requires energy: vesicles carrying the large enzyme molecules must move to and fuse with the plasma membrane to release their contents. Without ATP, this energy-requiring process cannot proceed normally, so less enzyme is released.

item.title: Solute Accumulation and Energy in Membrane Transport
item.stimulus:
Researchers studied how cells of a single-celled eukaryote take up solute X. They placed the cells in a solution in which the concentration of X was held constant at 2.0 mM. At the start, the cells contained no X. They then measured the concentration of X inside the cells over 30 minutes. One group of cells was untreated (control). A second group was treated with a compound that blocks ATP production but does not damage the plasma membrane. These cells also release a large digestive enzyme to their surroundings by exocytosis.

Time (min) | Internal X, control (mM) | Internal X, ATP blocker (mM)
0 | 0.0 | 0.0
10 | 2.0 | 1.2
20 | 4.5 | 1.9
30 | 6.0 | 2.0

External concentration of X in all trials: 2.0 mM
item.model_answer:
(a) Ratio = internal ÷ external = 6.0 mM ÷ 2.0 mM = 3.0. The control cells contain three times as much X as their surroundings.

(b) Active transport. At 30 minutes the control cells contain 6.0 mM X while the outside is only 2.0 mM, so X is being moved from a region of lower concentration to a region of higher concentration, against its gradient. This requires energy: when ATP production is blocked, the cells never rise above 2.0 mM, so the accumulation above the external level depends on ATP.

(c) In the ATP-blocked cells, X still moves by passive transport from the higher concentration outside (2.0 mM) to the lower concentration inside, which needs no direct input of metabolic energy. item.title: Passive, Active, and Bulk Transport in an Amoeba
item.stimulus:
A freshwater amoeba is a single-celled eukaryote. Researchers measured the concentrations of two small solutes, G and K, inside the amoeba and in the surrounding water. Both solutes show net movement into the cell.

Table 1
Solute | Concentration inside cell (mM) | Concentration in surrounding water (mM) | Direction of net movement
G | 0.8 | 6.0 | into cell
K | 25.0 | 1.5 | into cell

The researchers also added tiny plastic beads to the water. Each bead is far too large to pass through the plasma membrane. After 20 minutes, beads were found inside small membrane-bound vesicles in the amoeba's cytoplasm. The researchers then repeated the measurements on amoebas treated with a chemical that blocks the cell's supply of metabolic energy.

Table 2
Measurement | Untreated amoebas | Energy-blocked amoebas
Uptake rate of G (relative units) | 100 | 98
Uptake rate of K (relative units) | 100 | 3
Beads taken in per cell in 20 minutes | 40 | 0

parts.prompt: Using Table 1, explain why solute K must be moved into the cell by active transport.

criteria.text: Explains that K moves from a lower concentration outside (1.5 mM) to a higher concentration inside (25.0 mM), against its concentration gradient, and moving a substance from low to high concentration requires the direct input of energy (active transport).
criteria.evidence: Response cites K's concentrations (or states K moves from low to high concentration) and states that this movement requires an input of energy.
criteria.fix: Compare outside and inside concentrations; net movement from low to high concentration cannot be passive and requires energy input.

parts.prompt: Using Table 2, describe the evidence that solute G enters the cell by passive transport.

criteria.text: Describes that G's uptake rate is almost unchanged when the energy supply is blocked (100 versus 98), showing that G's net movement into the cell, from 6.0 mM outside to 0.8 mM inside, does not require a direct input of metabolic energy.
criteria.evidence: Response cites G's nearly unchanged uptake rate under the energy block (100 versus 98) as evidence that no direct energy input is needed.
criteria.fix: Compare each solute's rate with and without energy; a rate that barely changes shows the movement does not depend on metabolic energy.

parts.prompt: Describe how the plasma membrane brings the beads into the cell.

criteria.text: Describes endocytosis: the plasma membrane folds inward around the beads and pinches off, forming a new small vesicle that encloses them inside the cell.
criteria.evidence: Response describes the membrane folding in (or surrounding the beads) and forming a vesicle containing the beads; naming endocytosis or phagocytosis without describing the membrane movement is not enough.
criteria.fix: Describe the membrane's movement step by step: it folds in around the material, then closes off as a vesicle inside the cell.

parts.prompt: Inside the amoeba, undigested material is enclosed in vesicles that normally fuse with the plasma membrane to release the material outside the cell. Predict the effect of the energy-blocking chemical on the release of this material, and justify your prediction.

criteria.text: Predicts that release of the undigested material will stop or greatly decrease in energy-blocked amoebas.
criteria.evidence: Response states that the energy-blocked amoebas will release little or none of the material.
criteria.fix: State the direction of the change clearly: release stops, decreases, or stays the same.

criteria.text: Justifies that release by vesicle fusion is exocytosis, which requires energy (consistent with bead uptake by endocytosis falling from 40 to 0 when energy was blocked).
criteria.evidence: Response identifies the release as exocytosis (vesicle fusing with the membrane) and states that this process requires energy, optionally citing the bead data.
criteria.fix: Remember both endocytosis and exocytosis move large amounts of material in vesicles and both require an input of energy.

item.model_answer:
(a) Solute K is 1.5 mM in the surrounding water but 25.0 mM inside the cell, yet its net movement is into the cell. K is therefore moving from a region of low concentration to a region of high concentration, against its concentration gradient. Passive transport only produces net movement from high to low concentration, so moving K inward requires the direct input of energy: active transport.

(b) When the cell's supply of metabolic energy is blocked, the uptake rate of G stays almost the same (98 compared with 100), while the uptake of K drops to 3. G's movement into the cell therefore does not depend on a direct input of metabolic energy. This fits passive transport: G moves from high concentration outside (6.0 mM) to low concentration inside (0.8 mM).

(c) The beads enter by endocytosis. The plasma membrane folds inward around the beads, and the folded region closes and pinches off as a new small vesicle that contains the beads inside the cell.

(d) Release of the undigested material will stop (or nearly stop) in the energy-blocked amoebas. The material is released by exocytosis, in which a vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane, and exocytosis requires energy. The bead data show the same dependence for vesicle transport in the other direction: endocytosis fell from 40 beads to 0 when energy was blocked.
